<!--田辺市・上富田町)--> [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}} | image = [[File:Hayaoji.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Haya Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }}
'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== Inabane Oji === See the separate article on Inabane Oji.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}}.

This article covers members of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} in the region of {{ill|Tanabe City & Kamitonda Town|ja|田辺市・上富田町}} <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines-->
<!--田辺市・上富田町)-->
<!--田辺市・上富田町)--> [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}} | image = [[File:Hayaoji.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Haya Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }}
'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== Inabane Oji === See the separate article on Inabane Oji.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.
== References == - Ue, Toshikatsu (2004). *World Heritage Kumano Kodo*. Shinjuku Shobo. - "Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten" Editorial Committee (1985). *Wakayama Prefecture*. Kadokawa Shoten. - Koyama, Yasunori (2000). *Kumano Kodo*. Iwanami Shoten. - Nishi, Ritsu (1987). *Kumano Kodo Michishirube - Survey of the Current Status of Kujuku Oji*. Arao Seibundo. - Hasegawa, Yasutaka (2007). *Guidebook for Visiting Kumano Oji Shrines*. Shinpu Shobo. - Heibonsha (1997). *Encyclopedia of Temples and Shrines in Yamato and Kii*. Heibonsha.
== External Links == - [Kamitonda Town Cultural Property Classroom Series](http://www.town.kamitonda.lg.jp/section/kami50y/kami50y.html)
== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}}.
== Access == * '''Nearest Stations:''' {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, {{ill|Kii-Shinjō Station|ja|紀伊新庄駅}} (JR {{ill|Kisei Main Line|ja|紀勢本線}}) * Local bus services available via {{ill|Tanabe City Tourism Bureau|ja|田辺市熊野ツーリズムビューロー}}
== References == * 熊野路編さん委員会 (1973). *古道と王子社 - 熊野中辺路*. 熊野中辺路刊行会. * 西 律 (1987). *熊野古道みちしるべ - 熊野九十九王子現状踏査録*. 荒尾成文堂. * 平凡社 (1997). *大和・紀伊寺院神社大事典*. 平凡社.== See Also == * {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} * {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} * {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}}

<!--田辺市・上富田町)--> [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}} | image = [[File:Hayaoji.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Haya Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }}
'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== Inabane Oji === See the separate article on Inabane Oji.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}}.

<!--田辺市・上富田町)--> [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}} | image = [[File:Hayaoji.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Haya Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }}
'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|qq=Kujūku Ōji|qq=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== Inabane Oji === See the separate article on Inabane Oji.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}}.

<!--田辺市・上富田町)--> [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}} | image = [[File:Hayaoji.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Haya Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }}
'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|qq=Kujūku Ōji|qq=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

<!--田辺市・上富田町)--> [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}} | image = [[File:Hayaoji.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Haya Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }}
'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|qq=Kujūku Ōji|qq=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}}.

<!--田辺市・上富田町)--> [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}} | image = [[File:Hayaoji.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Haya Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }}
'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|qq=Kujūku Ōji|qq=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}}.

'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|qq=Kujūku Ōji|qq=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}}.

<!--田辺市・上富田町)--> [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)]] ==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}} | image = [[File:Hayaoji.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Haya Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }}
'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|qq=Kujūku Ōji|qq=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}}.

This article covers members of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} in the region of {{ill|Tanabe City|ja|田辺市}} & {{ill|Kamitonda Town|ja|上富田町}} <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines-->

==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}} | image = [[File:Hayaoji.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Haya Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }}
'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|qq=Kujūku Ōji|qq=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.
== References == - Ue, Toshikatsu (2004). *World Heritage Kumano Kodo*. Shinjuku Shobo. - "Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten" Editorial Committee (1985). *Wakayama Prefecture*. Kadokawa Shoten. - Koyama, Yasunori (2000). *Kumano Kodo*. Iwanami Shoten. - Nishi, Ritsu (1987). *Kumano Kodo Michishirube - Survey of the Current Status of Kujuku Oji*. Arao Seibundo. - Hasegawa, Yasutaka (2007). *Guidebook for Visiting Kumano Oji Shrines*. Shinpu Shobo. - Heibonsha (1997). *Encyclopedia of Temples and Shrines in Yamato and Kii*. Heibonsha.
== External Links == - [Kamitonda Town Cultural Property Classroom Series](http://www.town.kamitonda.lg.jp/section/kami50y/kami50y.html)
== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部}}.
== Access == * '''Nearest Stations:''' {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, {{ill|Kii-Shinjō Station|ja|紀伊新庄駅}} (JR {{ill|Kisei Main Line|ja|紀勢本線}}) * Local bus services available via {{ill|Tanabe City Tourism Bureau|ja|田辺市熊野ツーリズムビューロー}}
== References == * 熊野路編さん委員会 (1973). *古道と王子社 - 熊野中辺路*. 熊野中辺路刊行会. * 西 律 (1987). *熊野古道みちしるべ - 熊野九十九王子現状踏査録*. 荒尾成文堂. * 平凡社 (1997). *大和・紀伊寺院神社大事典*. 平凡社.== See Also == * {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰}} * {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}} * {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji}}

This article covers members of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|12=draft}} in the region of {{ill|Tanabe City|ja|田辺市|12=draft}} & {{ill|Kamitonda Town|ja|上富田町|12=draft}} <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines-->

==Overview== {{Shrine | Name = {{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)|12=draft}} | image = [[File:Hayaoji.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Haya Ōji Shrine]] | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町|12=draft}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県|12=draft}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō|12=draft}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰|12=draft}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = }}
'''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|qq=Kujūku Ōji|qq=Kujūku Ōji (田辺市・上富田町)|12=draft}}''' are a series of {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|12=draft}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市|12=draft}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|上富田町|12=draft}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=draft}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=draft}}.
== Overview == The Kujūku Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=draft}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=draft}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱|12=draft}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道|12=draft}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō|12=draft}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子|12=draft}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子|12=draft}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子|12=draft}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子|12=draft}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子|12=draft}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子|12=draft}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|12=draft}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子|12=draft}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子|12=draft}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=draft}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=draft}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.
== References == - Ue, Toshikatsu (2004). *World Heritage Kumano Kodo*. Shinjuku Shobo. - "Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten" Editorial Committee (1985). *Wakayama Prefecture*. Kadokawa Shoten. - Koyama, Yasunori (2000). *Kumano Kodo*. Iwanami Shoten. - Nishi, Ritsu (1987). *Kumano Kodo Michishirube - Survey of the Current Status of Kujuku Oji*. Arao Seibundo. - Hasegawa, Yasutaka (2007). *Guidebook for Visiting Kumano Oji Shrines*. Shinpu Shobo. - Heibonsha (1997). *Encyclopedia of Temples and Shrines in Yamato and Kii*. Heibonsha.
== External Links == - [Kamitonda Town Cultural Property Classroom Series](http://www.town.kamitonda.lg.jp/section/kami50y/kami50y.html)
== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家|12=draft}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|ja|和泉式部|12=draft}}.
== Access == * '''Nearest Stations:''' {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kii-Shinjō Station|ja|紀伊新庄駅|12=draft}} (JR {{ill|Kisei Main Line|ja|紀勢本線|12=draft}}) * Local bus services available via {{ill|Tanabe City Tourism Bureau|ja|田辺市熊野ツーリズムビューロー|12=draft}}
== References == * 熊野路編さん委員会 (1973). *古道と王子社 - 熊野中辺路*. 熊野中辺路刊行会. * 西 律 (1987). *熊野古道みちしるべ - 熊野九十九王子現状踏査録*. 荒尾成文堂. * 平凡社 (1997). *大和・紀伊寺院神社大事典*. 平凡社.== See Also == * {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰|12=draft}} * {{ill|Kumano Kōdō|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō|12=draft}} * {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|12=draft}}

This article covers members of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|12=draft}} in the region of {{ill|Tanabe City|ja|田辺市|12=draft}} & {{ill|Kamitonda Town|ja|上富田町|12=draft}} <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines-->
