This article covers members of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} in the region of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe City|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} & {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|WD=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda Town|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}
==Overview== {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | Name = {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3200280}} | image = File:Hayaoji.jpg | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|WD=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|lt=Wakayama Prefecture|1=Wakayama Prefecture}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰|1=Kumano Faith|2=ja|3=熊野信仰|WD=Q135501741}}{{efn|The religion of [[Kumano Shrines]]|1=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Three Shrines|lt=Kumano faith|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = | location = {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|1=Wakayama Prefecture}} | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|WD=Q455602|1=Amaterasu}} }}
'''{{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}}''' are a series of {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|WD=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haya Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City & Kamitonda Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11370052}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Detachi Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City & Kamitonda Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11370052}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Akitsu Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Maru Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Misu Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yagami Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinose Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayukawa Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== External Links == - [Kamitonda Town Cultural Property Classroom Series](http://www.town.kamitonda.lg.jp/section/kami50y/kami50y.html)
== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|WD=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|WD=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}}.

'''{{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}}''' are a series of {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|WD=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].

This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|WD=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|WD=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}}.

'''{{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}}''' are a series of {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|WD=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].

This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|WD=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|WD=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}}.

==Overview== {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | Name = {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3200280}} | image = File:Hayaoji.jpg | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|WD=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|lt=Wakayama Prefecture|1=Wakayama Prefecture}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰|1=Kumano Faith|2=ja|3=熊野信仰|WD=Q135501741}}{{efn|The religion of [[Kumano Shrines]]|1=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Three Shrines|lt=Kumano faith|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = | location = {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|1=Wakayama Prefecture}} | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|WD=Q455602|1=Amaterasu}} }}
'''{{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}}''' are a series of {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|WD=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haya Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City & Kamitonda Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11370052}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Detachi Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City & Kamitonda Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11370052}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Akitsu Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Maru Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Misu Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yagami Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinose Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayukawa Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|WD=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|WD=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}}.

These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].

This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|WD=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|WD=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}}.

This article covers members of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} in the region of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe City|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} & {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|WD=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda Town|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}
==Overview== {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | Name = {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3200280}} | image = File:Hayaoji.jpg | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|WD=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|lt=Wakayama Prefecture|1=Wakayama Prefecture}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰|1=Kumano Faith|2=ja|3=熊野信仰|WD=Q135501741}}{{efn|The religion of [[Kumano Shrines]]|1=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Three Shrines|lt=Kumano faith|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = | location = {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|1=Wakayama Prefecture}} | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|WD=Q455602|1=Amaterasu}} }}
'''{{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}}''' are a series of {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|WD=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q30074932}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|WD=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haya Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City & Kamitonda Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11370052}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Detachi Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City & Kamitonda Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11370052}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Akitsu Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Maru Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Misu Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yagami Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinose Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayukawa Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3149767}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== External Links == - [Kamitonda Town Cultural Property Classroom Series](http://www.town.kamitonda.lg.jp/section/kami50y/kami50y.html)
== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|WD=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|WD=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}}.

'''{{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}}''' are a series of {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|qid=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|qid=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q30074932}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|qid=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|qid=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].

This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3149767}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3149767}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|qid=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|qid=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}}.

This article covers members of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} in the region of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|qid=Q304266|lt=Tanabe City|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} & {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|qid=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda Town|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}
==Overview== {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | Name = {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3200280}} | image = File:Hayaoji.jpg | location = {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|qid=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}, {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|qid=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|Wakayama Prefecture|qid=Q131314|lt=Wakayama Prefecture|1=Wakayama Prefecture}}, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|41|00|N|135|22|00|E|region:JP|display=title}} | Affiliation = {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|qid=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}} - {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野信仰|1=Kumano Faith|2=ja|3=熊野信仰|qid=Q135501741}}{{efn|The religion of [[Kumano Shrines]]|1=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Three Shrines|lt=Kumano faith|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山}} | Established = 12th–13th century | Map = | location = {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|qid=Q131314|1=Wakayama Prefecture}} | deity = {{ill|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602|1=Amaterasu}} }}
'''{{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (田辺市・上富田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda, Wakayama|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}}''' are a series of {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} shrines located within the areas of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|qid=Q304266|lt=Tanabe, Wakayama|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}} and {{ill|Kamitonda, Wakayama|en|Kamitonda, Wakayama|qid=Q1346882|lt=Kamitonda, Wakayama|1=Kamitonda, Wakayama}}, Japan. These shrines were established primarily during the 12th and 13th centuries as protective sites for pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|1=Kumano Three Shrines|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10403700}}, particularly along the {{ill|Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kii route (Kumano Kōdō|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiiji|qq=}} and {{ill|Nakahechi route|ja|中辺路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakahechi route|1=Nakahechi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q30074932}}.
== Overview == The Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines were organized rapidly by {{ill|Kumano Shugen|ja|熊野修験|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shugen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135493040|1=Kumano Shugendo}} practitioners to guide and protect imperial and aristocratic pilgrims on their journeys to {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. After the decline of pilgrimages following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|qid=Q1372308|lt=Jōkyū War|1=Jōkyū War}} in 1221, many shrines fell into disrepair. Although some restoration efforts occurred during the Edo period, the modernization of Japan and the shift to {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} in the Meiji era led to the abolition or amalgamation of many shrines.
Today, the remnants of these shrines, including stone monuments and sacred groves, are preserved as part of the {{ill|Kumano Kodō|en|Kumano Kodō|qid=Q17050475|lt=Kumano Kodō|1=Kumano Kodō}}, designated as a [[National Historic Site of Japan]].
== Notable Ōji Shrines in Tanabe and Kamitonda == 1. '''{{ill|Haya Ōji|ja|芳養王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haya Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City & Kamitonda Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11370052}}''' – Located near the mouth of the Haya River, associated with eleven-faced Kannon. 2. '''{{ill|Detachi Ōji|ja|出立王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Detachi Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九十九王子 (田辺市・上富田町)|1=List of Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (Tanabe City & Kamitonda Town)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11370052}}''' – Known for ritual sea purification ceremonies before entering the mountains. 3. '''{{ill|Akitsu Ōji|ja|秋津王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Akitsu Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Historically moved due to flooding; its original site is now marked by a monument. 4. '''{{ill|Maru Ōji|ja|万呂王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Maru Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Located near rice fields known as Ōji Yashiki, possibly indicating an older shrine site. 5. '''{{ill|Misu Ōji|ja|三栖王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Misu Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Rebuilt after periods of neglect; its original location now holds remnants and a monument. 6. '''{{ill|Yagami Ōji|ja|八上王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yagami Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Mentioned in historical texts like *Sankashū*; known for the "Okano Shishimai" lion dance. 7. '''{{ill|Inabane Ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3149767}}''' – See dedicated article for details. 8. '''{{ill|Ichinose Ōji|ja|一ノ瀬王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinose Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – A significant site for water purification rituals along the Kumano River. 9. '''{{ill|Ayukawa Ōji|ja|鮎川王子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayukawa Ōji|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''' – Associated with historical legends and marked by commemorative monuments.
This article discusses the "Kujuku Oji" (Ninety-nine Shrines) located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town, Wakayama Prefecture.
== What is Kujuku Oji? == Kujuku Oji refers to a group of Shinto shrines along the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes, particularly along the Kiiji and Nakahechi routes. These shrines were rapidly organized mainly between the 12th and 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendo practitioners to serve as protective sites for pilgrims, especially members of the imperial family and nobility.
After the Jōkyū War in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many of these shrines. Despite efforts by the Kishu Domain during the Edo period to revive them, the shrines never regained their former prominence. The Meiji period's policies promoting State Shinto further contributed to the loss and merging of these shrines, leaving many sites unidentified or lost.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Oji shrines estimated to be located within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town.
== Kujuku Oji in Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town == There are nine Kujuku Oji shrines identified within Tanabe City and Kamitonda Town. See the separate article for Inabane Oji.
=== Haya Oji (Haya Grand Shrine) === Haya Oji is situated on a sand dune on the east bank of the Haya River estuary. Historical documents from 1792 identify its principal deity as Juichimen Kannon. This shrine has been known by various names in historical records, including "Haya Oji," "Hano," and "Hayano." It was revered as the guardian of the Haya region during the medieval period.
=== Detachi Oji === Located near Aizugawa's estuary, Detachi Oji is historically linked to saltwater purification rituals, an essential practice for pilgrims before proceeding inland. The shrine was eventually merged with Yatate Shrine in the early 20th century.
=== Akitsu Oji === Originally near the Aizugawa estuary, Akitsu Oji was relocated multiple times due to flooding. Historical records from 1201 mention it as "Akitsu Oji." The shrine was later known as Wakaichi Oji.
=== Maro Oji === Located southeast along the Aizugawa River, Maro Oji was referred to as "Maro Oji" in 1201 records. The shrine persisted until the Edo period.
=== Misu Oji === Situated on a hill east of the Aizugawa River, Misu Oji has also been known as "Misuzu Oji" and "Misu Yama Oji." The shrine fell into disrepair after the pilgrimage route shifted during the Edo period.
=== Yagami Oji === Yagami Oji is located at the foot of Mount Takabatake. Historical records suggest it was established shortly after 1109. The shrine experienced a revival in the late 17th century.
=== {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3149767}} === See the separate article on {{ill|Inabane Ōji|fr|Inabane-ōji|ja|稲葉根王子|lt=Inabane Ōji|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inabane Ōji|1=Inabane Ōji Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3149767}}.
=== Ichinose Oji === Ichinose Oji is located along the left bank of the Tonda River. Historical records from 1201 refer to it as "Ichinose Oji." The shrine was valued as a site for water purification rituals.
=== Ayukawa Oji === Ayukawa Oji, located north along the Tonda River, was merged with Sumiyoshi Shrine in 1874. Its original site no longer retains its historical features.

== External Links == - [Kamitonda Town Cultural Property Classroom Series](http://www.town.kamitonda.lg.jp/section/kami50y/kami50y.html)
== Cultural Significance == These shrines represent the fusion of Shinto and Buddhist practices unique to Kumano Pilgrimage culture. Many are associated with legends, poetry, and historical figures, such as {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|en|Fujiwara no Teika|qid=Q378425|lt=Fujiwara no Teika|1=Fujiwara no Teika}} and {{ill|Izumi Shikibu|en|Izumi Shikibu|qid=Q239898|lt=Izumi Shikibu|1=Izumi Shikibu}}.
